design_detail: EU own resource based on a progressive wealth tax for individuals or private households (A9-0155/2023 Amendment 2)
source_title: European Parliament roll-call vote 129, 10 May 2023: A9-0155/2023 Amendment 2
grading_note: Named in the affirmative roster (196 for, 383 against) of Amendment 2, which calls on the Commission to propose a new own resource based on a wealth tax for individuals or private households (paragraph 29a, amendment text read in the archived original).

design_detail: progressive tax on households with accumulated wealth over LVL 1 million (real estate, companies, vehicles, yachts)
quote_original: The new, progressive tax would be levied in households whose accumulated wealth – including real estate, companies they own, vehicles, luxury furniture, yachts, etc. – is estimated at over LVL 1 million.
grading_note: The association launched a signature drive for a named design (threshold and base stated), so a campaign with specifics. The source is a secondary news item (via LETA); the petition on manabalss.lv was not found, so a primary source would be an upgrade.

design_detail: Wealth tax on residents whose total value exceeds €1 million; basis and frequency unspecified
quote_original: Ieviesīsim bagātības nodokli valsts ierēdņiem un deputātiem, kuru ienākumi pārsniedz 50 tūkst. € gadā un iedzīvotājiem, kuru kopējā vērtība pārsniedz 1 milj. €
quote_en: We will introduce a wealth tax for civil servants and deputies whose income exceeds €50,000 a year and residents whose total value exceeds €1 million.
grading_note: Official election programme expressly calls for a wealth tax and gives a threshold; its meaning of total value, rate and frequency are not defined.

design_detail: Petition for a progressive 'millionaires tax' on household wealth above EUR 1 million, annual rates from 0.5% to 2%, with exemptions.
quote_original: Piedāvājam ieviest mērenu un progresīvu "miljonāru nodokli" ar gada likmēm no 0.5 līdz 2%.
quote_en: We propose introducing a moderate and progressive “millionaires tax” with annual rates from 0.5 to 2%.
grading_note: Named representative of an initiative that proposes annual taxation of household wealth across asset classes. Date is the page’s stated publication date, not verification of each current detail’s date. The petition page was read on 15 November 2026 and may have been edited since 2013, so the figures are those on the page today.

design_detail: Suggested 0.5% on net assets including land, gold and art; source does not state the frequency or threshold.
quote_original: Ideja ir tāda, ka nodoklis jāpiemēro cilvēka aktīvu — zelta, zemes, mākslas priekšmetu — neto vērtībai
quote_en: The idea is that the tax should be applied to the net value of a person’s assets—gold, land and works of art.
source_title: Former revenue director proposed introducing a wealth tax
grading_note: Direct attributed quotation describes an asset-stock tax; the report describes a 0.5% rate and deducting debts. Date refers to the original 31 January interview reported on 1 February.

design_detail: Podcast summary: 0.2–0.4% wealth tax above €1.5 million in property value; exact asset base and frequency not stated.
quote_original: bagātības nodoklis 0,2-0,4% tiem, kam īpašuma vērtība pārsniedz EUR 1,5 milj.
quote_en: Wealth tax of 0.2–0.4% for those whose property value exceeds €1.5 million.
source_title: Tax Stories episode 44: Kārlis Ketners on tax policy
grading_note: Podcast episode notes attribute this specific hypothetical tax design to Ketners; this is the host’s summary, not a verbatim transcript of his speech. Review: the 0.2-0.4% figures are the podcast host's summary of the episode, not Ketners's own words, so B until the episode itself is heard.

design_detail: Qualified support for introducing a wealth tax in Latvia; no preferred rate or threshold given.
quote_original: Pa daļai piekristu gan progresīvā ienākuma nodokļa, gan bagātības nodokļa ieviešanai
quote_en: I would partly agree with introducing both a progressive income tax and a wealth tax.
grading_note: Names a wealth tax and says he would partly agree; the surrounding answer raises ethical reservations, and the article discusses Norway’s wealth tax.
